statement: A sequence starts $a_1 = 3$, $a_2 = 5$, and each later term is the term before it divided by the term two places before it, that is $a_{n+2} = \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}$. What is $a_{2027}$?

choices.misconception: I worked with 2026 instead of 2027, which leaves remainder 4 on division by 6, so I took the 4th term.
I counted the first term as term 0, so remainder 5 pointed me to the sixth term of the cycle.
I thought the terms alternate, so every odd-numbered term would equal $a_1 = 3$.
I assumed the sequence repeats every 3 terms, and 2027 leaves remainder 2 on division by 3, so I took $a_2 = 5$.

hints: Work out the first eight terms carefully.
A rule applied again and again can bring back the starting pair of terms. Find the length of the cycle, then use the remainder of 2027 on division by that length.
The terms are $3, 5, \tfrac{5}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{5}, \tfrac{3}{5}, 3, 5, \dots$, so the cycle has length 6.

solutions.reliable: Compute: $a_3 = \frac{5}{3}$, $a_4 = \frac{5/3}{5} = \frac{1}{3}$, $a_5 = \frac{1/3}{5/3} = \frac{1}{5}$, $a_6 = \frac{1/5}{1/3} = \frac{3}{5}$, $a_7 = \frac{3/5}{1/5} = 3$, $a_8 = \frac{3}{3/5} = 5$. Since $a_7, a_8$ repeat $a_1, a_2$, and each term depends only on the two before it, the sequence repeats every 6 terms. As $2027 = 6 \times 337 + 5$, $a_{2027} = a_5 = \frac{1}{5}$. The transferable idea: when a two-term rule brings back the starting pair, the whole sequence is periodic and remainders do the rest.
solutions.elegant: For any start $a_1 = p$, $a_2 = q$, the rule gives $\frac{q}{p}, \frac{1}{p}, \frac{1}{q}, \frac{p}{q}$ and then $p, q$ again, so the period is always 6. Here $a_5 = \frac{1}{a_2} = \frac{1}{5}$.

whyOnTest: Recursive rules that bring back their starting values turn a question about term 2027 into a question about a remainder.
